lessons.title: Living Together in Peace — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
This unit teaches that people in a society depend on one another for safety, help and progress, so peaceful living is necessary. Peace brings cooperation and development, while conflict harms everyone and breaks trust.

The Charter of Madina

When the Holy Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) migrated from Makkah to Madina in 622 AD, he established the Charter of Madina. It laid down rules for living together among the Muslims, Jews and other tribes of Madina.

  • Every community was free to practise its own faith.
  • Disputes had to be settled fairly, and no community could oppress another.
  • All communities had to cooperate and defend the city together.

The Charter is still important today because it teaches inclusivity, tolerance, justice and cooperation wherever different communities live together.

Key Points

  • Peace is necessary because society members depend on one another.
  • The Charter of Madina was established on the Prophet's arrival at Madina.
  • Its lessons are inclusivity, tolerance, justice and cooperation.

lessons.title: Unit 1 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
Learn these words from Unit 1. They help you understand the lesson and the dictionary activity in the book.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
migrationMoving from one place to another to settle there.
inclusive societyA society where all communities, including minorities, enjoy equal rights, respect and protection.
accordAs a noun: agreement or consent, harmony between people. As a verb: to agree or be in harmony.
guidewordThe bold word at the top of a dictionary page; the first guideword is the first word on the page.
synonymA word with the same meaning, for example agreement and harmony for accord.
diversityPeople of different communities and faiths living in one society.

Example from the book: The neighbours lived in accord with one another and shared everything fairly.

Key Points

  • Migration in this unit means the Hijra to Madina in 622 AD.
  • Accord means agreement and harmony.
  • Guidewords stand at the top of a dictionary page.

lessons.title: Unit 1 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 1 teaches word building, kinds of nouns, kinds of sentences and the simple present tense.

Prefixes and Suffixes

  • un- means not: unfair, unkind, unknown, unhappy, unlucky.
  • re- means again: reread, rebuild, return, rewrite, replay.
  • -able means able to be: readable, washable, breakable, lovable.
  • -ed shows past tense: worked, played, learned, walked.
  • -en makes adjectives or verbs: wooden, golden, widen, strengthen.

Nouns, Sentences and Tense

  • Common noun: cars, dress, exams. Abstract noun: honesty. Collective noun: a bunch of grapes.
  • Four sentence kinds: declarative (statement), exclamatory (strong feeling), interrogative (question), imperative (command or request).
  • Simple present negative and questions use does not / Does with he, she or one name, and do not / Do with we, you or many: He does not play football. Does he play football?

Key Points

  • un- = not, re- = again, -able = able to be.
  • Honesty is an abstract noun; bunch is a collective noun.
  • With does, the verb returns to its first form.

chapters.title: Unit 2: Read and You Will Know

lessons.title: William Jones — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
This unit tells the story of William Jones, a boy who was incredibly curious about everything. He asked what clouds are made of, why rain falls, where rainwater goes, what makes the wind blow and why the sky is blue.

Read, and You Will Know

At first his mother answered his questions herself. When he learnt to read, she encouraged him to find the answers in books, saying, Read, and you will know. He could read quite well at the age of five.

By reading good books he became one of the most respected scholars of his time. The King of England made him a knight, Sir William Jones. He went to India as a judge of the Supreme Court, studied Sanskrit and Persian, and in 1784 founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal. He spoke and wrote twenty-eight languages, and his idea that Sanskrit, Latin and Greek share a common ancestry helped begin comparative linguistics.

Key Points

  • Curiosity and reading made William Jones a great scholar.
  • His mother's advice was: Read, and you will know.
  • He founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784.

lessons.title: Unit 2 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The book gives a word bank of difficult words from this unit. Learn their meanings and spellings for dictation.

Word Bank

WordMeaning
curiousEager to learn.
incrediblyTo a great degree.
dedicatedGiving full time and effort.
scholarA learned person.
foundedStarted an institution.
ancestryCommon origin.
comparative linguisticsThe study comparing languages.
inspiredFilled with the desire to do something good.

William Jones was a curious and dedicated scholar whose work inspired countless people to value education.

Key Points

  • A scholar is a learned person.
  • Founded means started an institution.
  • Ancestry means common origin.

lessons.title: Unit 2 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
The grammar exercises of Unit 2 teach the gender of nouns, three kinds of pronouns, and the difference between clauses and phrases.

Gender and Pronouns

  • Masculine: boy, actor. Feminine: girl, actress. Common: parent, student. Neuter: rock, table.
  • Subject pronouns do the action: They will be back. She went shopping. We bought chocolates.
  • Object pronouns receive the action: with us, to them, for him.
  • Possessive pronouns show ownership and stand alone: ours, yours, hers, mine, his.

Clauses, Phrases and Punctuation

  • A phrase cannot stand alone as a sentence: Once upon a time.
  • A clause has a subject and a verb: there was a boy named William Jones.
  • Punctuate with capital letters, full stops, commas and apostrophes, as in the paragraph about Sir William Jones.

Key Points

  • Parent and student are common-gender nouns.
  • Ours, yours, hers and mine are possessive pronouns.
  • A clause has a subject and a verb; a phrase does not.

lessons.title: Written in March — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
Written in March by William Wordsworth describes a beautiful spring morning after the rain, when winter is ending and nature looks fresh and joyful.

The Morning Scene

The cock is crowing, the stream is flowing, the small birds twitter, the lake glitters in the sun, and the green field sleeps in the sunshine.

Work and Life in the Fields

  • The oldest and the youngest are at work with the strongest.
  • Forty cattle are grazing, feeding like one, heads never raising.
  • The Ploughboy, the boy who ploughs the fields, whoops anon-anon, calling out again and again in joy.
  • There is joy in the mountains and life in the fountains.

The Snow Retreats

The snow has retreated like an army defeated and now survives only poorly on the top of the bare hill. At the end, the rain is over and gone, small clouds are sailing, and the blue sky is prevailing.

Key Points

  • The poem shows spring bringing new life after winter.
  • Nature and people are all full of joy and work.
  • The main idea: spring brings joy and beauty to the whole world.

lessons.title: Unit 3 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The poem uses old poetic words. Their meanings are given in the book from the context of the verses.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
crowingThe loud call made by a cock in the morning.
flowingMoving smoothly along, as water in a stream.
twitterThe short chirping sounds made by small birds.
glitterTo shine brightly with sparkling light.
grazingEating grass in a field.
retreatedMoved back or went away, as an army defeated.
prevailingExisting or spreading everywhere; dominant.
bareWithout covering, plants or leaves.

Sentences from the book: The lake doth glitter in the sun. The cattle are grazing in the green field. Blue sky is prevailing after the rain.

Key Points

  • Twitter is the chirping of small birds.
  • Retreated means moved back, like a defeated army.
  • Bare means without any covering.

lessons.title: Unit 3 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 3 teaches pronoun-antecedent agreement, the present continuous tense and the apostrophe with nouns.

Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement

A pronoun must agree with its antecedent, the noun it stands for: Saima was decorating her room. Aslam has driven his car carefully. The dog is playing with its tail. I have accomplished my task.

Present Continuous Tense

  • Form: is, am or are + verb-ing. He is playing football.
  • Negative: He is not playing football.
  • Interrogative: Is he playing football? Are we studying science?

Apostrophe with Nouns

  • The child's toy, the baby's smile — one owner.
  • The boys' college, the teachers' lounge — plural owners ending in s.
  • The children's books, women's rights — plural owners not ending in s.

Key Points

  • A pronoun agrees with its antecedent.
  • Present continuous = is/am/are + verb-ing.
  • The apostrophe shows ownership with nouns.

lessons.title: Disaster Management — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
A disaster is an unexpected and sudden event that causes serious harm, like an earthquake, a flood or a storm. There are two kinds: natural disasters, from natural events, and human-made disasters, from human mistakes like factory explosions. Epidemics and wars are also disasters.

What Is Disaster Management?

Disaster management is the process of preparing for and responding to disasters. It means organizing resources to prevent, prepare for, respond to and recover from disasters, so harm to lives, health and property is reduced.

  • Learn about hazards and make a family disaster plan.
  • Know shelter locations and evacuation routes.
  • Do not build schools and hospitals in flood-prone areas.
  • Relief means shelters, food, water and first aid for affected people.

Key Points

  • Disasters are sudden, unexpected and destructive.
  • Preparation and planning reduce the harm.
  • Safety is a shared responsibility of all.

lessons.title: Unit 4 — Word Meanings and Grammar
lessons.notes_html:
This short lesson covers the key words of Unit 4 and its one grammar activity, the apostrophe.

Words and Meanings

  • disaster — a sudden event causing serious harm, like an earthquake or flood.
  • earthquake — a sudden shaking of the ground caused by movement of the earth's crust.
  • disaster management — preparing for and responding to disasters in an organized way.
  • relief — help given after a disaster, like shelters, meals, water and first aid.

Apostrophe in a Paragraph

The activity adds apostrophes where necessary: Sameer's family visited the park. The birds' cages were beautiful. The apostrophe shows belonging or a shortened form.

Key Points

  • An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground.
  • Relief includes shelter, food, water and first aid.
  • Sameer's and birds' show the apostrophe in use.

chapters.title: Unit 5: Do Good and Keep It Doing

lessons.title: Do Good and Keep It Doing — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Every day a woman baked an extra chapatti, placed it on the window sill for whoever would take it, and prayed for her son who had gone far away to seek his fortune.

The Hunchback

Every day a hunchback took the chapatti and said, The evil you do remains with you; the good you do comes back to you! He never said a word of gratitude. Annoyed, the woman once mixed poison in the chapatti. But her hands trembled, she felt guilty, threw the poisoned chapatti into the fire and baked a fresh one.

The Good Comes Back

That evening her son returned, thin, weak and hungry. A mile from home, the hunchback had given him his whole chapatti, saying his need was greater. The mother understood: if she had not burnt the poisoned chapatti, her own son would have eaten it and died.

Key Points

  • Moral: the good you do comes back to you.
  • Do good and keep doing it, even without thanks.
  • Good deeds have consequences, good or bad.

lessons.title: Unit 5 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
These words and pairs come from the story and its vocabulary activities. Learn what each one means in the book.

Story Words

  • chapatti — the flat bread the woman baked every day and placed on the window sill.
  • window sill — the place at the window where she kept the chapatti for a needy person.
  • gratitude — thankfulness; the hunchback never expressed a word of gratitude.
  • tattered and torn — the son's garments were worn out and damaged when he returned.

Binomial Pairs

  • black and white — the old photograph was in black and white.
  • day and night — the nurse worked day and night.
  • pros and cons — the good and bad points of a plan.
  • give and take — both sides helping each other in a friendship.

Key Points

  • Binomial pairs are two words joined by and.
  • Gratitude means thankfulness.
  • Tattered and torn describes the son's clothes.

lessons.title: Unit 5 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 5 teaches phrasal verbs, idioms, homophones, homographs and the present perfect tense.

Word Pairs That Confuse

  • Phrasal verbs: blow up, call off (cancel), set up, break down.
  • Idioms: lend a hand (help), hit the hay (go to sleep), piece of cake (very easy), break the ice (start talking).
  • Homophones sound the same but differ in meaning: to, too, two; son, sun; flower, flour; right, write; see, sea.
  • Homographs are spelled the same but sound and mean differently: lead, tear, bass, bow, wind.

Present Perfect Tense

  • Form: has or have + third form of the verb. She has played hockey.
  • Negative: She has not played hockey.
  • Interrogative: Has she played hockey? Have you helped the poor?

Key Points

  • Homophones sound alike; homographs are spelled alike.
  • Present perfect = has/have + third form.
  • Call off means cancel; piece of cake means very easy.

lessons.title: Going Forward — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
Going Forward is a poem about moving ahead in life with good values. The poetess asks to be taught the right quality for every hard moment of life.

What She Asks to Be Taught

  • When there is anger — teach me patience, to wait calmly.
  • When there is injustice — answer with strength, to stand up for what is right.
  • When there is need — teach me compassion, kindness for those who need help.
  • When there is sadness — answer with empathy, sharing the feelings of others.
  • When there is noise — give me silence, to be calm and peaceful.

Feel, Heal and Share

The second stanza allows every feeling its place: laughter in joy, tears in grief, forgiveness in guilt, healing in hurt and growth in change. In the last stanza she advises us to share ideas about the future, share lessons from the past, discover new horizons and live in harmony.

Key Points

  • Anger needs patience; injustice needs strength.
  • Need needs compassion; sadness needs empathy.
  • Share past lessons and live together in harmony.

lessons.title: Unit 6 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The poem is built on pairs of problems and good qualities. The book explains each quality in simple words.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
patienceWaiting calmly instead of acting in anger.
strengthThe power to stand up for what is right against injustice.
compassionKindness and care for others who need help.
empathyUnderstanding and sharing the feelings of others.
forgivenessLetting go of guilt and anger towards someone.
harmonyLiving alongside one another in peace.
horizonA new limit or new possibility to discover, in new horizons.

Remember the pairs: anger with patience, need with compassion, sadness with empathy, noise with silence.

Key Points

  • Compassion is kindness for those in need.
  • Empathy is sharing the feelings of others.
  • Harmony means living together in peace.

lessons.title: Unit 6 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 6 teaches simple and compound sentences, adjectives made from nouns, and adjectival phrases.

Simple and Compound Sentences

  • A simple sentence has one complete idea: She loves to read. The cat is sleeping.
  • A compound sentence joins two ideas with but, and or so: She loves to read, but she also enjoys writing. He runs every morning, so he stays fit.

Adjectives from Nouns

  • question + able = questionable
  • nature + al = natural
  • child + ish = childish
  • storm + y = stormy
  • colour + ful = colourful

Adjectival Phrases

Groups of adjectives describe a noun together: the big green plastic bin, the cool green grass, the hard working girl.

Key Points

  • Compound sentences join ideas with but, and or so.
  • Suffixes like -able, -al and -ful make adjectives.
  • Adjectival phrases describe a noun.

chapters.title: Unit 7: The Autobiography of a Piece of Paper

lessons.title: The Autobiography of a Piece of Paper — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
An autobiography is the story of a life written by the person himself or herself. In this unit, a piece of paper tells its own life story.

From Tree to Paper

The paper began as part of a tall, green tree in the forest. The tree was cut down, its wood was chopped and ground with water into a mushy mixture called pulp. The pulp was cleaned, spread into thin sheets, pressed with rollers, dried and cut into paper.

Life in School and Old Age

  • In school it was used for homework with maths problems and spelling words.
  • Children drew pictures on it, cut shapes and folded origami.
  • It was also used for letters to family and friends.
  • As it grew old, its edges became worn, it turned a little yellow, its ink faded and it developed small creases.

Key Points

  • Paper is made from the wood of trees.
  • Pulp is ground wood mixed with water.
  • Old paper turns yellow and gets creases.

lessons.title: Unit 7 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
These words come from the paper's own story. Each meaning is taken from how the book explains the word.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
autobiographyThe story of a person's life written by that person himself or herself.
pulpThe mushy mixture made by grinding chopped wood into tiny bits and mixing them with water.
origamiPaper folded into shapes, as children folded it in art projects.
wornDamaged by much use; the old paper's edges became worn.
creasesSmall fold lines; the old paper developed creases from being handled often.
recycledUsed again in a new form after the first life is over.

Steps to remember: tree, chopped wood, pulp, thin sheets, pressed, dried, cut into paper.

Key Points

  • An autobiography is written by the person himself.
  • Pulp is ground wood mixed with water.
  • Recycling gives old paper a new life.

lessons.title: Unit 7 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 7 teaches imperative sentences, useful expressions, relative pronouns, articles and sentence structures.

Imperatives and Relative Pronouns

  • Positive imperative tells someone to do something: Please be quiet. Always respect your elders.
  • Negative imperative tells someone not to do something: Do not forget. Never leave your luggage unattended.
  • Relative pronouns: whose for possession (the artist whose paintings), who for people (the student who scored highest), which or that for things (the car which was parked).

Articles and Sentence Structures

  • Use an before vowel sounds: an accident, an onion. Use a: a thousand dollars, a pen. Use the for a known thing: the truth, the book I gave you.
  • SVO: She eats an apple. SV: Birds fly. SVA: He is happy; She runs quickly. SVN: She studies science.

Key Points

  • Whose shows possession; who is for people.
  • An comes before vowel sounds.
  • SVO means Subject, Verb, Object.

chapters.title: Unit 8: The Mountain and The Squirrel (Poem)

lessons.title: The Mountain and the Squirrel — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
This poem tells of a quarrel between a huge mountain and a tiny squirrel. The mountain, proud of its great size, called the squirrel a Little prig.

The Squirrel Answers

The squirrel replied calmly. The mountain is doubtless very big, but all sorts of things and weather must be taken in together to make up a year and a sphere. It is no disgrace for the squirrel to occupy its own small place.

  • If I am not so large as you, you are not so small as I, and not half so spry.
  • Talents differ; all is well and wisely put.
  • If I cannot carry forests on my back, neither can you crack a nut.

The Lesson

Every creature and thing has its own value. The mountain can carry forests but cannot crack a nut; the squirrel can crack a nut but cannot carry forests. Pride in size or strength is foolish, and small does not mean unimportant.

Key Points

  • The world needs everything, great and small.
  • Talents differ from creature to creature.
  • Small does not mean unimportant.

lessons.title: Unit 8 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The squirrel uses a few special words in its answer. The book explains them through the poem itself.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
quarrelAn argument; the mountain and the squirrel had a quarrel.
prigA small, conceited creature; the mountain called the squirrel a Little prig.
spryQuick and lively; the mountain is not half so spry as the squirrel.
disgraceShame; the squirrel feels no disgrace in its small place.
sphereThe whole round world, made up with all things and weather together.
talentsDifferent abilities given to each creature.

The famous line to remember: If I cannot carry forests on my back, neither can you crack a nut.

Key Points

  • A prig is a conceited creature.
  • Spry means quick and lively.
  • Talents differ in every creature.

lessons.title: Unit 8 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 8 teaches figures of speech, kinds and degrees of adjectives, comparison clauses and relative clauses.

Figures of Speech and Adjectives

  • Personification: the mountain and squirrel speak and quarrel like human beings.
  • Hyperbole: carrying forests on my back is an exaggeration for effect.
  • Kinds of adjectives: quantity (much, many), shape (rectangular), origin (American), quality (excellent), size (tiny), colour (red).

Degrees and Clauses

  • Comparative: heavier than, better than. Superlative: the worst decision, the most expensive piece.
  • Comparison clause: She sings more sweetly than her sister does.
  • Relative clause: The dog that lives next door barked loudly. I bought a phone which has a good camera.

Key Points

  • Personification gives human actions to things.
  • Heavier and better are comparative forms.
  • Relative clauses begin with that, which or where.

lessons.title: The Secret of Happiness — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
A shopkeeper sent his son to learn the secret of happiness from the wisest man in the world. After wandering through the desert for 40 days, the boy reached a beautiful castle full of activity and waited two hours to meet the wise man.

The Spoon with Two Drops of Oil

The wise man gave him a teaspoon with two drops of oil and asked him to wander in the palace for two hours without spilling the oil. The first time, the boy kept his eyes fixed on the spoon and saw nothing — not the Persian tapestries, not the garden made in ten years, not the parchments in the library. He felt embarrassed.

The Second Tour

The second time he saw all the marvels: works of art, gardens, mountains and flowers. But when he looked down, the oil was gone. Then the wise man told the secret: see all the marvels of the world and never forget the drops of oil on the spoon.

Key Points

  • Happiness needs balance between enjoyment and duty.
  • The marvels mean life's beauty; the oil means our duties.
  • Enjoy the world, but never neglect responsibilities.

lessons.title: Unit 9 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
These words name the marvels of the palace and the lesson of the story, as the book describes them.

Words and Meanings

  • marvels — the wonderful things of the world: works of art, gardens, mountains and flowers in the palace.
  • tapestries — the Persian cloth artworks hanging in the palace, one of its marvels.
  • parchments — the old writings kept in the library of the castle.
  • orchestra — the small group playing soft music inside the castle.
  • embarrassed — ashamed; the boy felt this when he had seen nothing on his first tour.
  • entrusted — given into someone's care; the wise man asked where the drops of oil he had entrusted to the boy were.

The whole story turns on one pair: the marvels of the world and the drops of oil on the spoon.

Key Points

  • Marvels are the wonderful things we enjoy.
  • The drops of oil stand for our small duties.
  • Entrusted means given into someone's care.

lessons.title: Unit 9 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 9 teaches do, does and did as helping and main verbs, modal verbs, and the past perfect tense.

Do, Does, Did and Modals

  • As main verbs: They do their work in time. She does her job sincerely. He did his work well.
  • As helping verbs: They do not read story books. She does not eat junk food. He did not work hard.
  • Modal verbs: can for ability (She can write stories), should for duty (We should recite daily), may for permission or possibility (May I come in?).

Past Perfect Tense

  • Form: had + third form. She had finished her homework before class.
  • Negative: She had not finished her homework.
  • Interrogative: Had she finished her homework? Had the train departed by then?

Key Points

  • Do and does can be main or helping verbs.
  • Can shows ability; should shows duty; may shows permission.
  • Past perfect = had + third form of the verb.

chapters.title: Unit 10: Artificial Intelligence in Our Daily Lives

lessons.title: Artificial Intelligence — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a way to make machines think and act like humans. Computers learn from experience and data, solve problems and even make decisions, to imitate human abilities and make our lives easier.

AI Around Us and Its Benefits

  • Voice assistants like Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant answer questions and play music.
  • Online shopping websites recommend products we have looked at or bought before.
  • Benefits: efficiency, accuracy, personalization, safety and twenty-four-hour availability through chatbots.

Concerns and Careful Use

AI can make mistakes when data is missing or wrong, it cannot fully understand human emotions, and it raises concerns about privacy, job displacement and bias. We must use it ethically: respect privacy, check decisions for bias, make clear rules and keep human control over important decisions.

Key Points

  • AI makes machines think and act like humans.
  • It learns by using data to find patterns.
  • Use AI ethically and keep human control.

lessons.title: Unit 10 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The benefit and concern words of this unit are explained in the book itself, in brackets and answers.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
efficiencyTasks done faster.
accuracyFewer human errors; better diagnoses.
personalizationLearning plans made for each student.
safetyProtection, as in self-driving cars and factories.
privacyKeeping personal data safe from misuse.
biasUnfair decisions learnt from biased data.
job displacementSome jobs changing or disappearing because of AI.

AI learns by using data to find patterns — that is why wrong or biased data can lead it to wrong or biased decisions.

Key Points

  • Efficiency means tasks done faster.
  • Bias means unfair decisions from biased data.
  • Personalization means plans for each student.

lessons.title: Unit 10 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 10 teaches compound words, adverb phrases, prepositions, gerunds and participles.

Compound Words and Adverb Phrases

  • Compound words join two words: ice-cream, football, bookshelf, rainbow, butterfly, sunflower, moonlight, raincoat, firefly.
  • Adverb phrase of manner: with determination. Of time: before dawn. Of place: under the old oak tree. Of frequency: twice a week. Of degree: extremely tired.

Prepositions, Gerunds and Participles

  • Position: on the table, under the bed. Time: at 3 o'clock, on Monday. Movement: towards the park, over the fence. Since March; for two years.
  • Gerund: verb-ing used as a noun — Swimming is my favourite hobby.
  • Participle: verb form used as an adjective — the running water, the broken vase.

Key Points

  • Bookshelf and rainbow are compound words.
  • A gerund works as a noun; a participle as an adjective.
  • Since shows a starting point; for shows a period.

lessons.title: The World — The Poem in Simple Words
lessons.notes_html:
In The World, the poet looks at our great, wide and beautiful Earth and feels very small before it.

The Wonderful World

  • The wonderful water is curled round the Earth.
  • The wonderful grass is upon its breast, like a dress.
  • The wonderful air is over us, and the wonderful wind shakes the tree, walks on the water, whirls the mills and talks to itself on the tops of the hills.
  • There are wheat-fields that nod, rivers that flow, and cities, gardens, cliffs and isles, with people for thousands of miles.

Small, Yet Greater

The poet trembles: Ah, you are so great, and I am so small. But while saying his prayers, a whisper inside gives the comforting thought of the last two lines: You are more than the Earth, though you are such a dot: You can love and think, and the Earth cannot!

Key Points

  • The Earth is great, wide, beautiful and wonderful.
  • A human is tiny, like a dot, beside the Earth.
  • Yet humans are greater, because they can love and think.

lessons.title: Unit 11 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
The poet repeats the word wonderful for everything he sees. Learn the poem's special words as the book explains them.

Words and Meanings

  • wonderful — great and beautiful; the poet calls the water, grass, air and wind wonderful.
  • curled round — wrapped around; the wonderful water is curled round the Earth.
  • breast — the front surface of the Earth in the poem's picture, wearing grass like a dress.
  • whirls — turns round quickly; the wind whirls the mills.
  • isles — islands; the Earth has cities, gardens, cliffs and isles.
  • dot — a tiny point; a human being is such a dot beside the vast Earth.
  • trembles — shakes with awe; the poet trembles to think of the World at all.

The most important pair in the poem is great Earth and small human — and the human still wins, because he can love and think.

Key Points

  • Wonderful is the poem's key repeated word.
  • A dot means a tiny point, the small human.
  • Whirls means turns round quickly.

lessons.title: Unit 11 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 11 teaches direct and indirect speech: how to report what someone said, with and without their exact words.

Identifying the Two Forms

  • Direct speech gives the exact words inside quotation marks: They said, We have won the match. The boy said, I like to fly a kite.
  • Indirect speech reports the words with that, if or whether: Sara said that she was reading a storybook. He asked me if I was busy.

Changing into Indirect Speech

  • Raza said, I live in a village. — Raza said that he lived in a village.
  • She said, I am going out. — She said that she was going out.
  • Questions use if: My father asked if it was raining outside. Obaid asked if I read the newspaper.
  • The tense usually moves one step back: live to lived, am going to was going, is crying to was crying.

Key Points

  • Direct speech uses quotation marks and exact words.
  • Indirect speech uses that for statements.
  • Indirect questions use if, without a question mark.

lessons.title: The Paddle Boat — Summary
lessons.notes_html:
Two boys, Robert and Christopher, were fishing in a small river from a heavy flat-bottomed boat, each holding a long, crooked rod and waiting for a bite.

A Better Way Than Poling

To move the boat they had to pole it, pushing a long pole against the bottom of the stream. Robert thought poling was slow and hard — the old boat crept no faster than a snail — and there ought to be a better way. His idea: fit the boat with paddle wheels turned by a crank.

Building and Steering

  • They made two rough but strong paddle wheels of wood.
  • An iron rod passed through the boat from side to side, bent in the middle as a crank; each wheel was fastened to an end of the rod.
  • For steering, Robert fastened something like an oarlock at the stern, with a paddle working in it.
  • Christopher's father was impressed and pleased with the invention.

Robert kept planning and working on new ideas, and as a man Robert Fulton became famous for inventing the steamboat, with paddle wheels run by steam.

Key Points

  • Poling was slow, hard work.
  • Paddle wheels turned by a crank moved the boat.
  • Robert Fulton later invented the steamboat.

lessons.title: Unit 12 — Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
These words name the parts of the boys' invention and the old way of moving the boat, exactly as the story explains them.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
polingPushing against a long pole whose lower end reaches the bottom of the stream, to move a boat.
paddle wheelsWheels fixed on the sides of a boat that push it forward through the water.
crankThe bent middle part of the iron rod, turned by hand to move the wheels.
oarlockThe fitting at the stern that held the steering paddle.
sternThe back part of the boat, where Robert fastened the oarlock.
steamboatA boat with paddle wheels run by steam, invented by Robert Fulton.

Robert's complaint to remember: the old boat crept over the water no faster than a snail — that is, extremely slowly.

Key Points

  • Poling means pushing a pole against the stream bed.
  • The crank turned the paddle wheels.
  • The steamboat's wheels are run by steam.

lessons.title: Unit 12 — Grammar Points
lessons.notes_html:
Unit 12 teaches conjunctions, transitional devices, the past continuous tense and the past perfect tense.

Conjunctions and Transitional Devices

  • because: She did not go to the concert because she had to work late.
  • and / or: Finish this report and go. Tea or coffee?
  • but / although: He is good at math but struggles with science. We can go although it rains.
  • However: Jameel loves swimming. However, he is afraid of deep water. As a result: I forgot my umbrella. As a result, I got soaked.

Past Continuous and Past Perfect

  • Past continuous: was or were + verb-ing. He was playing football. Negative: He was not playing. Question: Was he playing?
  • Past perfect: had + third form. I had bought the tickets before the movie started. The train had departed when I arrived.

Key Points

  • Because gives a reason; however shows contrast.
  • Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing.
  • Past perfect = had + third form.
